sections.h2: What makes selling in Reading different
sections.html:
Reading is a dense, rowhouse-heavy city where a sale needs a city Certificate of Transfer, carries a transfer tax of 5%, and often involves a house that has not been updated in decades. Those three facts shape price, timing and who is likely to buy.

Housing costs are far below the Philadelphia suburbs, and most households rent. The buyer pool leans toward investors, rehab buyers and first-time owners. Sellers here usually weigh a repair-and-list route against a quick sale to an investor, and the sections below show what each route requires at the city and county level.

With only about four in ten homes owner-occupied, a large share of Reading's houses are rentals. Owners of those properties also deal with the city's housing registration and rental inspection cycle, which matters if tenants are in place at the time of sale.

The seller must obtain this city document before a sale closes, and it applies to every property sold in Reading regardless of use. The seller applies before the sale and hands the buyer a property packet with summary sheets.

A Health and Safety Inspection that checks code compliance is part of the process. Either the buyer or the seller may arrange it, and the city allows limited exemptions. The forms are a Certificate of Transfer and Property Sale Inspection Application, and a Property Sale Inspection Acknowledgement.

  • Download the sale application from the city's Housing Welcome Packet page and complete it as early as the sales agreement is signed.
  • Ask the City of Reading Property Maintenance division, which works from 815 Washington Street, for the current fee and processing time.
  • Agree in the sales contract who schedules the inspection and who pays for any violations it finds.
  • For help or complaints, the Citizen's Service Center is at 1-877-727-3234.

A seller who sells as-is to an investor should still get the certificate lined up. It is a city requirement, so it does not disappear because the buyer is paying cash.

sections.h2: Transfer tax in the City of Reading
sections.html:
The transfer tax rate is 5% in the City of Reading, compared with 2% in every other Berks municipality. One percent of that goes to the state, and the Berks County Recorder of Deeds collects the whole amount when the deed is recorded.

Pennsylvania law makes both parties liable, so the sales agreement should say who pays and how it is split. Settle that before the contract is signed, since it is a real negotiating point on a lower-priced house.

  • Personal checks are not accepted for transfer tax at the Recorder's office, and cash is no longer accepted either.
  • The base recording fee for a deed is $88 for up to four pages, with $4 for each additional page.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) goes with any deed that leaves the full price off. The Common Level Ratio on that form is 3.12 for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
  • The Recorder of Deeds is in the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, third floor, phone 610-478-3380.

Certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt under state law, so an inherited house passing to an heir may owe nothing.

Reading homeowners are assessed through Berks County and pay the county, the city and the Reading School District. Call Berks County for the current millage on your parcel, and ask the Berks County Assessment Office for the appeal deadline and form, since the rules for contesting a value are set at the county level.

Call the Berks County Tax Claim Bureau about any unpaid years. A title company will request a tax certification before closing, and unpaid taxes are paid from sale proceeds.

The city's code program adds its own tickets. Reading's Quality of Life program issues immediate tickets that increase with repeat violations at the same property in a year, and the city holds blight hearings for deteriorated properties. Clearing open violations before closing keeps them from becoming a buyer's negotiating point.

sections.h2: List, repair or sell to a cash buyer
sections.html:
The answer depends on condition and timing. A house in good repair near a historic district may do well on the open market, but a vacant rowhouse with deferred maintenance may be worth more to a rehab investor than to a retail buyer who needs financing.

  • Get a rough repair estimate before listing. Many Reading buyers use loans that require inspections and appraisals.
  • Work out your net after the 5% transfer tax, the sale inspection, commissions and unpaid taxes.
  • If you own rental units, ask the Property Maintenance office how registration and open inspection findings pass to a new owner.
  • If time matters more than price, a cash sale on an as-is basis avoids lender delays, though the Certificate of Transfer is still required.

sections.h2: Steps from signed contract to closing
sections.html:
Start the paperwork on day one. Pull together the deed, recent tax bills and any city notices, then work down this list.

  1. Download and complete the Certificate of Transfer and Property Sale Inspection Application as soon as the sales agreement is signed.
  2. Decide in writing whether you or the buyer books the Health and Safety Inspection, and who pays for violations it turns up.
  3. Fix or disclose open code items. A violation the city has recorded does not go away at closing.
  4. Ask the closing agent to request the tax certification from the county and to confirm unpaid years with the Tax Claim Bureau.
  5. Agree on how the 5% transfer tax is split, and have the title company bring the deed to the Recorder with the tax paid by check.

Selling as-is for cash drops the mortgage appraisal and lender timeline. The city certificate and the inspection still apply, so your closing date hinges on how fast those two get done.

sections.h2: Selling with tenants or open violations
sections.html:
You can sell a Reading house with code violations, but the sale inspection will surface them, and the contract must say whether you repair them or the buyer does. A vacant or deteriorated property can also draw a blight hearing, so addressing it before you list protects your price.

For a rental, confirm the housing registration is current and read the lease before you accept an offer. An investor buyer will want to know the rent, the lease end date and whether inspection findings are open.

faqs.q: Is a Certificate of Transfer required for every house sale in Reading?
faqs.a: Yes. The certificate is necessary for all properties sold in the city regardless of use, with limited exemptions only from the Health and Safety Inspection. The seller applies before the sale.

The law makes buyer and seller jointly liable, and the sales agreement decides who actually pays. The Berks County Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording, at 5% in the City of Reading versus 2% elsewhere in Berks.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Reading house with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes, but the sale inspection will surface them, and the contract must say whether you repair them or the buyer does. Open violations that the city has recorded do not go away at closing.

faqs.q: Does an inherited house in Reading owe transfer tax?
faqs.a: Property passed by will or intestate succession is exempt from realty transfer tax under state rules. A later sale by the heir to a third party is a normal taxable transfer at the Reading rate.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed after a Reading sale?
faqs.a: At the Berks County Recorder of Deeds, third floor of the Services Center at 633 Court Street in Reading, or by e-recording through a title company. Your closing agent usually handles it and pays the transfer tax by check.
